halfway|us.t: Switched from Monarch and haven't looked back
halfway|us.c:
We tried Monarch for about six months. Great app but it treated us like one financial unit. Everything was shared, everything was visible, and we kept arguing about who spent what on personal stuff. We earn different amounts too so the whole thing felt off from the start.
Halfway is different. Shared expenses are tracked together, personal spending stays private. The split adjusts based on what we each earn so I'm not overpaying relative to my income anymore. Settlement screen tells us exactly who owes what at the end of the month. No spreadsheet, no calculator, no argument. Free to start which was the other thing. Monarch is $99 a year. Halfway costs nothing until you want bank sync.

I’ve tried pretty much every budgeting app out there - YNAB, Mint, Monarch, Goodbudget, Splitwise - and Halfway is the only one built specifically for couples managing shared expenses. It does one thing really well instead of trying to be everything to everyone.

The proportional splitting feature is what sold me. Most apps assume you split everything 50/50, but Halfway lets you split based on income percentages. You set it once and every shared expense automatically splits the right way. No manual calculations, no spreadsheets, just done.

What really impressed me is the flexibility. You can set different split percentages for different categories. For example, you might want to split groceries one way and rent another way. Or some expenses can be 50/50 while others are proportional. Most apps force you into one rigid system, but Halfway adapts to however you and your partner actually handle money.
The privacy features are excellent. You can mark transactions as shared or personal, and personal spending stays completely private. Your partner can't see what you spend on personal stuff unless you choose to share it. This is huge - other couples apps I tried either showed everything to both people or made it way too complicated to separate shared vs personal.

Transaction tracking is smooth. Adding expenses is quick, categorization works well, and the settlement feature shows exactly who owes what at any time. No more "wait, did I pay you back for that?" conversations. One button settles everything up.
The budgeting tools are solid too. You can set budget limits by category and both people see the same progress. It's collaborative without being controlling, which is a hard balance to strike.

A few things could be better - the recurring bills tracker is good but could be smarter about detecting patterns, and the mobile app occasionally lags when loading transactions. Also wish there was a desktop web version for when you want to do deeper analysis.

But overall, this is the first budgeting app I've actually stuck with for more than a few months. It's not bloated with features I don't need, and it solves the specific problem of managing shared finances fairly. The UI is clean and modern, not overwhelming like some of the older apps.

If you've been tracking shared expenses in Notes or a spreadsheet, or if you're using apps that weren't built for couples, give Halfway a shot. The free version has everything you need to get started. Premium adds automatic bank sync which is worth it if you hate manual entry.

Pro tip: take a few minutes to set up your categories and split percentages properly at the start. Once that's configured, everything runs on autopilot and you barely have to think about it.

Definitely recommend, especially if you're managing money with a partner and want something that actually understands how couples handle finances.

Before Split Pay, payday often felt like a temporary sigh of relief instead of something I could truly enjoy. I would get paid, take care of my biggest bills, and then spend the rest of the week trying to stretch whatever was left. As a working mother, there was always something that needed to be paid for, whether it was household expenses, groceries, gas, something for my child, or an unexpected expense that never seemed to come at the right time.

Split Pay changed the way I manage my money by allowing me to divide larger expenses into smaller, more manageable payments. Something so simple made a huge difference. Instead of one bill taking such a large portion of one paycheck, I could spread the responsibility out and still have room to take care of my family’s everyday needs.

The biggest change wasn’t just financial. It was the peace of mind. I stopped feeling like I was constantly trying to catch up. I could breathe a little easier knowing that my responsibilities were being handled without sacrificing everything else in between paydays.

Split Pay didn’t magically make my bills disappear or give me more money. What it gave me was balance, flexibility, and a sense of control over the money I already worked hard for. Sometimes changing someone’s life doesn’t require a huge financial windfall. Sometimes, it’s simply giving them a better way to manage what they already have.

For me, Split Pay did exactly that, and that little bit of breathing room made a much bigger difference than I ever expected.

splitpay-bills-in-two|us.t: Review is long but will help you
splitpay-bills-in-two|us.c:
I applied for Split Pay hoping it would help with flexible payments on a larger purchase, but the entire process left me disappointed and frustrated. Despite having a solid, steady income well above what they advertise as qualifying thresholds — as a self-employed fiber optic contractor running my own crews and business — I was denied approval right away.

The application was 
straightforward at first, but the denial came without any clear explanation. Like most companies, they’ll claim it’s based on “many factors,” but it’s pretty obvious that a credit check plays a heavy role here. 

It feels misleading when income requirements are promoted but don’t seem to carry much weight if your credit score isn’t perfect.
I understand these services have risk models, but for someone with verifiable income and a real business, it would be helpful to have more transparency instead of the generic “many factors” response. 

This experience made me question whether Split Pay is truly designed for working professionals and small business owners like me, or if it’s mainly for those with pristine credit histories.
Would not recommend based on my experience. 

((((If your credit is strong, you might have better luck — but don’t count on income alone getting you approved.))))
